item.title: Fins Up, Fins Down | Winners and losers from Miami Dolphins Week 10 defeat
item.description: Michael Taaffe gets third interception while Dolphins’ special teams continues to struggle.
item.content:encoded:
The Miami Dolphins traveled to Indianapolis to take on the Colts on Sunday — and despite a spirited effort from an injury depleted squad that nearly eeked out their second victory on the season, the South Florida squad fell to their opponents by a score of 24-22. Unfortunately, Dolphins’ former kicker Zane Gonzalez missed two field goals and an extra point attempt in the loss — a performance that cost him his job on Monday.

While the result wasn’t a positive one for the standings, it does keep Miami in the running for the first overall pick in the 2027 NFL Draft. The Dolphins are currently third — sitting behind the winless Los Angeles Chargers and the single-win Tennessee Titans in the draft order. Losing to the Colts hurts the New York Jets’ draft stock, as they own the Colts’ first round selection due to the Sauce Gardner trade during the 2025 season. So, there’s your silver-lining.

FINS UP

Our Fins Up player of the week is rookie safety Michael Taaffe. Taaffe intercepted a Daniel Jones pass in the second quarter of Sunday’s loss, giving him a team-leading three interceptions on the season. The fifth round pick in the 2026 NFL Draft has vastly outplayed his draft position thus far, giving Miami a player with game-changing ball skills in the secondary at a discount.

Don’t look now, but Taaffe could soon find himself in the Defensive Rookie of the Year award conversation as he is currently tied for the league lead when it comes to most interceptions by a rookie defender this season. Will he win? Probably not, but having multiple players in the running (Jacob Rodriguez) is a very good thing for the future of Miami’s defense.

FINS DOWN

Our Fins Down personality is once again Special Teams coordinator Chris Tabor. As mentioned above, Miami’s former kicker Zane Gonzalez missed two field goal tries and an extra point try against the Colts. Those missed kicks cost the Dolphins a win and Gonzalez his job. However, his coach, Tabor, still remains employed despite burning through two kickers (Riley Patterson) this season, while also being the leader of a unit that has consistently ranked in the bottom-five of all special teams units in the NFL this season.

In a year when wins and losses don’t necessarily mean as much as they would if the Dolphins were considered a viable contender for a playoff spot, Tabor keeping his job isn’t the end of the world, but general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan does have an opportunity to show his coaching staff, players, owner and fans of the franchise that he means business when it comes to preparation equaling production on game days. Let’s see if he takes it.

item.title: 10 thoughts on the Cowboys loss to the 49ers
item.description: The Cowboys have no answers for anybody right now.
item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys suffered a disappointing 46-40 home loss to the San Francisco 49ers in what turned out to be a super high-scoring affair. Despite teasing us with an early lead and staging an interesting fourth-quarter comeback, defensive breakdowns and explosive plays ultimately derailed the team’s hopes. Here are 10 thoughts on the game.

1. False hope early

Many expected the 49ers offense to roll right out of the gate, yet the Cowboys defense surprisingly kept things close early. After allowing an opening-drive touchdown, the defense forced a three-and-out and then held the 49ers to a field goal, jumping ahead 16-10 with 4:08 left in the first half. For a fleeting moment, it actually looked like they had a real chance.

2. The onslaught

As great as things were early, the game got out of hand quickly. Starting late in the second quarter and carrying into the fourth, the 49ers went on a 28-3 run with four drives of 75 yards or more. The Cowboys’ defense was hanging on for dear life on every possession, and whatever magic they had working for them early completely fell apart.

3. Death by big plays

This game featured over 1,000 total yards, with the 49ers racking up 584 of them, the most Dallas has allowed since Week 10 in 2013. Against a highly efficient offense, the Cowboys repeatedly fell victim to massive chunk plays. Christian McCaffrey broke loose for touchdown catches of 74 and 66 yards, while Deebo Samuel added a 70-yard touchdown. Any time the Cowboys felt like they might pick up a little steam, one of these guys would have a big play that just let the air out of AT&T Stadium.

4. Duel threats

The 49ers offense is an enigma because you never know where the damage will come from next. On Sunday, their top playmakers swapped traditional roles, as wide receiver Deebo Samuel finished as their leading rusher while running back Christian McCaffrey led the team in receiving. Of course, those numbers got a massive boost from the big plays the defense surrendered.

5. Purdy escapes trouble

San Francisco’s quarterback Brock Purdy was precise, throwing for 389 yards, three touchdowns, and zero turnovers while completing 79% of his passes. Beyond making one smart decision after another, Purdy repeatedly escaped the pocket to hit his targets on the run. He consistently turned near-stops for the Cowboys into monumental gains for the 49ers. What a cotton-headed ninny-muggins.

6. The pressure’s on

While Purdy scrambling out of trouble hurt the Cowboys, the defensive front still deserves credit for harassing him all afternoon. Most of the heat came right up the middle, resulting in five sacks, the most Purdy has taken all season. Five different defensive tackles got a piece of the action. Five. That’s crazy. All the DTs are making plays. It’s a group effort.

7. Dak airs it out

A balanced attack was never going to cut it against the 49ers, so the Cowboys wisely took to the air. Dak Prescott attempted 51 passes, completing 30 for 343 yards and five touchdowns. His lone interception came on fourth down when he launched it downfield instead of running for the sticks, marking the only time the offense was stopped in the second half. Of course, one false step is all it took for the game to fall out of reach.

8. Welcome back, GP

The Cowboys got a huge lift from the return of George Pickens, who hauled in 11 catches for 145 yards and three touchdowns. He and 49ers cornerback Deommodore Lenoir battled all afternoon, exchanging shots throughout the contest. Pickens proved nearly impossible to guard, and the only thing that really slowed him down was his own taunting penalty.

9. Fourth-quarter surge

Trailing 38-19 in the fourth quarter, the game looked finished until the offense sparked a rally with three straight touchdown drives, each taking three minutes or less. After cutting the deficit to 38-32 with under four minutes left and all three timeouts remaining, the Cowboys just needed one more stop. Sadly, they didn’t get it. Instead, it took the 49ers less than 20 seconds to crush any remaining hope that existed.

10. Clean game

Brian Schottenheimer catches plenty of deserved flak, yet he did nothing to hurt his team on Sunday. Penalties were down, and his aggressive fourth-down calls paid off with four conversions, even if a fake-snap charade briefly toyed with our emotions. Going for two when they were trailing eight points late in the fourth was also the right call, giving his team a chance to win the game had they somehow found the end zone one last time.

item.title: Super Bowl Coach Applauds Jaguars’ Jordan Davis, Jessie Bates Trades
item.description: A SuperBowl-winning coach weighs in on the Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates acquisitions. Are the Jaguars SuperBowl ready?
item.content:encoded:
When a Super Bowl-winning head coach, with a strength in defense praises your recent defensive roster moves, it’s probably worth paying attention. NBC analyst Mike Tomlin, who won a Super Bowl during his 19 seasons leading the Pittsburgh Steelers, had a few glowing remarks when discussing the Jacksonville Jaguars adding safety Jessie Bates III and defensive tackle Jordan Davis on last week’s NBC conference call:

“I think they helped themselves in two distinct ways from a defensive perspective and so it’s a sign that they’re all in. It’s really impressive and it’s going to be fun to watch.”

I fully agree with Tomlin here. The resulting roster outlook following the moves, the clear championship aims from the 7-2 Jaguars, and the limited risk exposure, while improving in two areas of defense turned last week’s trade deadline into clear roster improvements.

With the deadline dust now settled, we take a quick look at why the trades make Jacksonville’s second-ranked defense (in points surrendered) significantly better, and why the money behind the moves may be the most underrated part of the story.

Jordan Davis: Filling the DHam Void

The case for Davis starts with what Jacksonville lost. According to NextGenStats, the Jaguars’ defense allowed 6.9 yards per play in 2026 when Davon Hamilton was off the field and just 3.8 when he was on it. Some of that gap reflects the fact that Hamilton didn’t play on obvious passing downs, but it also shows just how dominant he was against the run. A similar pattern shows up with Ventrell Miller, whose splits are 3.16 yards per carry allowed with him on the field and 5.66 with him off. A 3.1-yard swing in yards per play shows how much Hamilton mattered, and why Jacksonville, with Hamilton hurt for the remainder of the season in Week 8, needed a real replacement to keep its Super Bowl hopes intact.

Davis is clearly that replacement. He led the Eagles with a 67.4 percent double-team rate this season while playing mostly on first and second downs, and PFF still graded him as the best defensive tackle in Philadelphia’s group on those downs. Notably, he had only 52 pass-rush snaps over eight games because that was, frankly, not his role.

In Anthony Campanile’s defense, the run defense has to be elite: not good and not merely above average. This is a team that wants to play nickel, dime, and three-safety sets, and stopping the run on early downs is what keeps opponents in second and third-and-long. Davis does that, and then some. Limiting opponents on early downs forces them to throw into a defense expecting the pass and gives additional opportunities to a defense that already ranks among the league’s top three in interceptions. It is a scheme with a long track record, one that worked for years for Vic Fangio, with whom Campanile has history.

Speaking of interceptions…

Jessie Bates: More Than Just a Ballhawk

Jacksonville added a magnet for the football to a defense that already ranks among the league’s interception leaders. Bates also forces fumbles at a remarkable rate, with three this season, and he’s scored a defensive touchdown in four straight seasons, including this one.

The most important part of his arrival, though, is how he fits Campanile’s love of coverage variety. All offseason, the missing piece for this defense was a rangy, sideline-to-sideline safety who can patrol the middle of the field for Cover 3 and Cover 1, the looks Jacksonville prefers in the red zone. Bates is that player. In many ways, he just turned a top-five red zone defense into a Madden cheat code. With Travis Hunter and Montaric Brown outside, Jarrian Jones and Jourdan Lewis working the slots, and Bates roaming center field, there is potential for even more third-down Cover 1, even outside the red zone. While one defender may occasionally require additional help when playing man outside the red zone, Jacksonville would clearly hold the man-to-man advantage when lining up against most receiving groups.

There is also a part of Bates’s game that people have probably not considered. The secondary lost its “Foye Oluokun of the back end” in Eric Murray, the communicator who makes sure everyone lines up correctly and avoids coverage busts. That is also the most underrated part of Bates’s game. He is not only a superior athlete to almost everyone around him. He is a student of the game who communicates and studies tape, something we covered in the 5 Questions About Jessie Bates article with The Falcoholic’s Jeanna Kelley:

Jessie Bates is obsessed with film study. He carries two iPads around the facility — one from the team with that week’s game plan information loaded on it, and his personal device for taking notes and looking up specific plays, etc.

From Bates, via AtlantaFalcons.com: “Film study has always been my way of separating from other players,” Bates said. “That’s what I love. That’s the part a lot of people don’t see every day – the grind, the amount of time that you put into film to shine and make plays on Sunday.”

Easing Them In

Neither Bates nor Davis played Sunday against the Tennessee Titans. Following the midweek trades, Jacksonville opted to give both players the week to rest and acclimate. The decision made sense given the circumstances: neither player had a 2026 bye week with his previous team, and Bates had only just returned from Santiago Bernabéu Stadium in Madrid, where Atlanta faced the Cincinnati Bengals. A week to recharge and to continue the crash course into Campanile’s system seems a worthwhile investment with the stretch run still ahead.

The Money Made Sense

What may get lost in the pick-by-pick conversation is how well the contracts work with Jacksonville’s current limitations. Between the two deals, Jacksonville saves around $25 million over the next two years. In effect, the Jaguars bought two years of salary relief by agreeing to part with higher draft capital to secure top players at their position at a low cost. The Eagles absorbed the $19 million prepaid bonus they had given Davis over two years, and the Falcons paid almost all of the $6.5 million owed to Bates in 2026. That leaves $25 million in immediate funds that Jacksonville can put toward extensions for wide receiver Parker Washington or safety Antonio Johnson, rather than being forced to restructure contracts to create cap space. Jacksonville did not say “F— them picks.” It used picks as currency to buy exactly what it wanted at a discount in salary. Essentially, they used a coupon, and closed that deal while reportedly bidding against the Buffalo Bills for both players.

Godchaux & the Comp-Pick Game

While not mentioned by Tomlin, the Jaguars also added defensive tackle Davon Godchaux, which gives them more interior depth. The savvy move with Davon is that he allows Jacksonville to play the compensatory pick game, as he’s on an expiring contract. That is similar to what the team did with Greg Newsome in 2025, with Jacksonville likely to receive a sixth-round pick for him in this coming draft.

Jacksonville’s conditional 2028 sixth-round pick traded for Godchaux accelerates to a 2027 sixth once awarded to the Jaguars by the NFL. However, if Davon were to perform well, Jacksonville could either re-sign him to an extension or allow him to test free agency, where if he signs a reasonable free-agent deal this offseason, there’s a non-zero chance the compensatory formula rewards Jacksonville with a late-round pick right back. In other words, Jacksonville could trade a 2027 sixth-round pick for a player, get half of a year’s usage out of that player at a $650k cap hit, and turn around and receive a 2028 sixth- or seventh-round pick right back. And if the trade doesn’t work out in the long term, Godchaux provides functional depth, at a cheap salary, for the cost of a sixth-round selection as the worst-case scenario. It’s a true low-risk scenario.

Good Business All Around?

Between the two bigger trades, Jacksonville swapped Murray’s safety spot for a more versatile, more dominant one with fewer coverage limitations, and replaced the defensive tackle spot with a younger, more dominant player. Added to the Godchaux move, this all just seems to be good business on all three trades. They improved upon their already turnover-happy secondary, while also improving their top-of-the-league run defense.

But even for those who may not consider the costly trades to be “good value”, it’s easy to see why they were constructed in the way that they were (IE: how we got here). While the national media slams the trades, I think many missed the details when looking solely at the picks, while avoiding the money and existing cap limitations in Jacksonville.

But what say you, BigCatCountry? Do you agree or disagree with Tomlin? Where do you stand on the risk versus reward of the moves?

Download the SB Nation App and drop your thoughts below!

item.title: After Further Review: New York Jets- Buffalo Bills
item.description: How was the officiating for the Jets-Bills game?
item.content:encoded:
After each game, we’ll be sharing a comprehensive review that breaks down some of the controversial decisions from the officiating crew in the game. You may disagree in some cases, and that’s fine…

Penalty Count

Bills 7-35 (leading to zero Jets first downs)
Jets 7-53 (leading to two Bills first downs)

Note: This does not include penalties that are declined or off-set.

Plays where the call was obvious, uncontroversial or not visible on broadcast footage

Jets Penalties

  • Defensive holding on Kingsley Enagbare on 3rd-and-goal at the one-yard line. There is no argument here as Enagbare, who was initially engaged as he would have been assuming his man was a blocker, had a fistful of jersey as the receiver tried to get away from him.
  • Offensive holding on Joe Tippmann to negate a 19-yard Garrett Wilson catch. There was a loss of leverage here and his man beat him into the backfield while he was still reaching across and holding on, so this was probably reasonable.
  • Olu Fashanu false start. Flinch before the snap.
  • Too many men on the field on 1st-and-goal at the nine-yard line. Not sure what happened here, but Breece Hall seemed to be the only player who came off the field after it. You can say it had an impact because Hall caught a 10-yard pass two plays later which would have been a touchdown.
  • Malik McClain holding penalty to negate a nice Isaiah Davis kickoff return. Lost leverage and pulled his man back, then dragged him to the ground.
  • Armand Membou false start. Not sure about this one, as no movement from Membou or any other Jet was obvious from broadcast footage.

Bills Penalties

  • Michael Hoecht offside on a punt. Jumped early. This took it from 4th-and-6 to 4th-and-short but the Jets were too close to their end zone to risk going for it.
  • Ed Oliver neutral zone infraction, also on 4th-and-6. Reacted to the hard count. This time the Jets converted on the next play.
  • Dawson Knox false start. Went very slightly early as the ball was being snapped.
  • Dion Dawkins false start on a field goal. Well spotted by the officials as Dawkins shifted his weight before the ball was snapped.
  • Offside on Bradley Chubb. Went early. This didn’t matter because Wilson caught a 25-yard pass anyway.
  • Alec Anderson false start. Big flinch before the snap.
  • Illegal shift on 3rd-and-7. Basically had two men in motion at the same time as the ball was snapped. Certainly neither was set for a full second.
  • Hoecht offside again. Went early, but again it didn’t matter as Breece Hall ran for a first down.
  • Spencer Hawes false start. Flinched, reacting to the right tackle moving but because he wanted to turn around and clarify something with Josh Allen.

Plays that require further discussion

Jets Penalties

  • Malachi Moore defensive pass interference. There was some hand-fighting going on here but it looked for all the world like Moore made every effort NOT to grab or impede the receiver’s ability to make the catch. It was reminiscent of one of those NBA plays where the person with the ball deliberately tucks his defender’s arm under his own to create the illusion of defense-initiated contact.
  • Offensive pass interference on Mason Taylor to negate a 45-yard catch-and-run for Isaiah Williams. Collided with the defensive player trailing Williams on a crosser. In real time, it looked like Taylor changed direction and made a bee-line for the defensive player when the design of this play calls for him to make his initial route look naturally like it just happened to get in his way a bit. However, to a degree, it’s possible Taylor’s man was leaning on him a bit, perhaps cognisant of what was happening, which forced him into a collision. As for the defender Taylor blocked off, you need to contrast this with what Azareye’h Thomas did last week. In a similar situation, he actively avoided the contact and went around the defender, leading to a 31-yard gain, instead of letting the contact happen and drawing the flag. That’s likely because he knows there’s a chance they won’t get the call, whereas the Bills player was obviously confident he would.

Bills Penalties

  • Illegal use of the hands on Davison Igbinosun. This was on the same play where Williams long catch-and-run did not count, and offset the Taylor flag. There was fairly incidental contact on Adonai Mitchell’s facemask but the Jets had a couple of big ones similar to this, including one on Thomas that negated an interception against the Bears. The difference here is that the receiver did not initiate the contact by leaning or ducking into the attempted jam as was the case on those two Jets penalties.

Notable no-calls etc

Here were some of the other notable missed calls, replay situations and controversial moments:

  • Brandon Stephens’ early third down stop on James Cook was correctly marked short and also correctly not ruled as a fumble as his elbow hit before the ball was jarred loose. The fumble rolled out of bounds for what would have been a couple of yards loss to prevent it from being a makeable 4th-and-1.
  • It goes without saying that every Bills’ tush push was a textbook example of “assisting the runner” but the NFL has turned a blind eye to that for years. The Jets ran their own, which didn’t have anything as egregious as Dalton Kincaid literally shoving Allen like a grocery cart across the line to gain.
  • DJ Moore wanted pass interference on Stephens downfield early on but the no call was probably right. Stephens was leaning a hand on Moore quite a bit though, which isn’t a great habit even if you’re not actively preventing him from going in the direction he wants to.
  • On the play where Omar Cooper got hurt, the block was legal as he timed it right after the pass was released. However, there could have been two penalties on the Bills here – a facemask on the player who tackled Kenyon Sadiq and an illegal hands to the face call on the play who shoved Cooper back.
  • There was no defensive pass interference on the deep ball that Geno Smith underthrew to Mitchell. If only it was a worse underthrow – then Mitchell would have been drawn into Christian Benford, whose head was not turned, to create obviously flaggable contact.
  • The electronic measurement system, which is pointless anyway because it still uses the official’s on-field spotting of the ball, had Cook marked less than an inch short on one play.
  • The officials overlooked a blatant bear-hug by O’Cyrus Torrence on Harrison Phillips on a short yardage conversion. He literally had him wrapped up to prevent him from getting lateral, but you get away with these kinds of things on the interior.
  • On Khalil Shakir’s jet sweep, Keon Coleman had his hand on the outside of Moore’s shoulder, pulling him back slightly from getting outside. He did let go of this pretty quickly, though.
  • Brown flinched slightly before one of Buffalo’s successful sneaks and the officials did not notice.
  • Benford had early contact with two hands on Wilson on a high throw to the pylon before half time. Under the old rules maybe that was uncatchable but that’s not a thing these days.
  • The controversial hit on Smith had Aaron Glenn saying there’s no way they don’t make the same call if it was Josh Allen and he has a point. The difficulty here is that Smith initially starts to run and then sets and throws. To be clear on the rules, you’re not a defenseless player if you are attempting to run outside the pocket, but a helmet-to-helmet hit can still be called on a non-defenseless player. Additionally, he did ultimately throw the ball so roughing the passer can still be called even though he is outside the pocket. This could have been a flag if there was a low hit, but in this instance the Bills player was initially going in for the tackle and actively tried to roll away from contact as he saw the throw coming out. However, there could also be roughing for a late hit, or forcible contact to the head/neck area. There could also be a launching penalty because the player making the hit had one foot off the ground as he propelled himself at Smith. Maybe he led with the shoulder, maybe initial contact was below the neck area but the fact there was obvious forcible contact, a launch component and incidental contact to the head/neck after the initial hit means there was enough here to draw a flag. If you’re Josh Allen. (Regardless of what Gene Steratore says).
  • Minkah Fitzpatrick had a hit on Allen near the sideline but it wasn’t late and was a two-handed shove to the chest, so that shouldn’t have been flagged and in this case wasn’t.
  • Membou had his helmet knocked off again but, once again, didn’t get a call for illegal hands to the face. It looked clear that Oliver caused this by shoving at his chinstrap and the lower part of his facemask.
  • One no-call that went in the Jets’ favor was Wilson pushing off at the top of his route to make a first down catch.
  • It looked like Kincaid might have gone out of bounds further upfield on his long catch-and-run but he actually stayed in.
  • Another hit on Smith that could have been flagged was when Cole Bishop dived at him to knock him down. This wasn’t a particularly dangerous or forceful hit, and wasn’t that late, but he easily could have pulled out of the hit and, as we know from the likes of Steratore trying to justify marginal-looking calls against the Jets in the past, that should lead to a penalty (for example the one on David Bailey a few games ago). There was also a launch component, although he led with the hands.
  • On his touchdown catch, Moore was worried he might have fumbled before he broke the plane and unsuccessfully scrambled to get it back. It was not a problem, because he had broken the plane. In addition, he didn’t need to complete the catch to prevent an incompletion before going to ground because he took 4-5 steps with the ball before losing it. Had this happened in the field of play rather than the end zone it would be a fumble, rather than an incompletion.
  • The Bills also wanted a hit on a defenseless receiver call against Fitzpatrick and were probably unlucky not to get it. Fitzpatrick came in clean and led with the shoulder at a contact point around the back/shoulder area. However, when you come in upright with that much force, there is usually some incidental contact up high. This was on the play where the Bills were called for an illegal shift.
  • On his interception, you may have wondered if Thomas could have got up and run had he not been injured because it didn’t look like he was down by contact. However, Greg Dortch’s foot made contact with his hand on the way down, so he would have been ruled down.
  • Mitchell had a catch overturned by the replay booth. He’s usually adept at those sideline toe-tappers but in this case the Bills player shoved him out before he landed so his second foot came down out of bounds.
  • Finally, Cade Klubnik had a weird play where he was about to be sacked but pitched it towards Taylor for an apparent incompletion. However, the officials had blown it dead. He was never down, and “in the grasp” is no longer a thing, but presumably they would say his forward progress had been stopped.

Let us know what we missed – or misinterpreted – in the comments…

item.title: Mendoza, Raiders get punched in face the by visiting Seahawks 21-13
item.description: Losing tight end Brock Bowers early, ineffective run game compound rookie’s 1st start; defense cooked in 2nd half
item.content:encoded:
For two quarters and the first possession of the third quarter, the Las Vegas Raiders held a precarious 10-7 advantage against the visiting Seattle Seahawks this past Sunday.

But that opening second-half possession was a sign of the avalanche that was coming. It as a three-and-out series where the Silver & Black netted negative two yards. That showcased the second-half adjustments Mike Macdonald’s Seahawks made to walk out of Allegiant Stadium 21-13 victors.

“I’ve got to give the Raiders a lot of credit,” Macdonald said. “In the first half, I thought they had a good plan. They made it challenging for us in the first half. Our guys did a great job adjusting and sticking together and finding a way to win in the end.”

Realizing the Raiders were starting a rookie quarterback in Fernando Mendoza and without all-world tight end Brock Bowers — who injured his ankle early in the first quarter and returned to the game, only to exit in the second quarter — Macdonald dialed up the pressure resulting in four-second half sacks. All of those arrived in the fourth quarter with the Raiders in catchup-mode and neither head coach and offensive play caller Klint Kubiak or Mendoza had an answer.

“I thought overall when we lost Brock, you definitely saw a big change in production. So I look at myself; I have to do a much better job of moving the ball, getting and spreading the ball around,” Kubiak said after the game.

“Yeah, Seahawks have a fantastic defense. We’ve seen it all season, so a lot of credit to them and Coach Macdonald. Fantastic,” Mendoza said after the game. “And it’s good to get punched in the face because now it’s a great opportunity to grow and learn and to really unveil all the deficiencies that I have in my game, as a future hopeful leader of this offense.”

Like Mendoza said above, dissecting the game tape and learning from this battering he received from Seattle’s defense is integral for Las Vegas going forward. How the quarterback takes the hard lessons learned facing a top NFL defense going forward in the Raiders remaining seven games — four of which are AFC West clashes — will dictate the future of the Silver & Black.

Mendoza did get walloped quite a bit by the Seahawks aggressive defense but he took the hits and kept getting back up. Surely his 6-foot-5 and 225-pound frame helps absorb that punishment but seeing their franchise quarterback getting rocked isn’t ideal.

To his credit, Mendoza shouldered the blame for the sacks for holding on to the ball too long and not getting rid of it absolving his offensive linemen of the blame. The accountability for the No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft is endearing, but absolution has no business in the Raiders locker room, despite what the 23-year-old signal caller said at the podium.

The ineffectiveness on offense was offensive and it was only a matter of time before the Seahawks offense found some rhythm to take advantage of the Raiders much-maligned defense.

With the impotence from Kubiak’s offense to open the second half, Seattle engineered an eight-play, 87-yard touchdown drive to jump ahead 14-10. And, after another three-and-out where Las Vegas could only gain a single yard before punting, the Seahawks hit the jackpot play: Elite (and arguably the best) wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba’s freelance sprint that left Raiders linebacker Quay Walker and cornerback Eric Stokes in the dust for a 71-yard catch-and-run touchdown.

Let’s hit the quick slants as fast as JSN had the Raiders defense in a blender:

—Raiders edge rusher Maxx Crosby powered the team’s defensive effort with eight total tackles, four stops for loss, and a sack. But unlike Mendoza, who was sacked six times and hit 12 times, Seahawks quarterback Drew Lock was sacked and hit three times, respectively.

—Seattle nickel cornerback Devon Witherspoon paced the Seahawks defense with two sacks while DeMarcus Lawrence, Byron Murphy II, Dante Fowler, and Derick Hall each had a sack. Witherspoon and Lawrence paced Seattle with three quarterback hits, each.

—Lock finished 14 of 17 for 240 yards and two passing touchdowns. He also added 20 yards on six carries. Running back Zack Charbonnet paced Seattle’s ground game with 20 carries for 94 yards. Rookie Jadarian Price had nine totes for 36 yards and a touchdown.

—Las Vegas pitiful run game was powered by Mike Washington Jr. who finished with eight carries for 23 yards (2.9 yards per carry average). Fellow tailback Ashton Jeanty had nine carries for 18 yards (2.0 yards per carry) and tight end Michael Mayer had one carry for two yards.

—The Raiders avoided setting a new modern era record of allowing 30 or more points for the seven-straight game. Instead the team is tied for that awful record in six-straight contests. But allowing 150 rushing yards and 232 air yards to the Seahawks ailing offense wasn’t ideal.

—Mendoza, meanwhile, finished 17 of 29 for 143 yards passing with no touchdowns or interceptions. He added 22 yards on six carries including his first-career touchdown — a 10-yard run that was a play similar to the one he scored on during Indiana’s national title win last season.

Quote of Note

“Yeah, in the second half, because of how the game was going, our defense did a fantastic job, but because of how we were playing offensively, at the forefront myself, we got behind there, and so it’s a little bit more of a passing situation. And then Coach (Mike) Macdonald dialed it up and did great. There was a couple times that we tried to check someone else’s protection, and he was playing chess, and he fooled me, and he got me a couple times. And I think it’s important to learn and grow from this, to throw my hot routes more often, to throw accurate balls when getting hit, and to practice that rather than everything just being sunshine and rainbows, then move forward and give our team a better chance each and every week.”

—Las Vegas Raiders rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza on the second-half performance

“He got up after every hit. … He’s a tough dude. He’’s ready to fight, right? And it should piss us off when he’’s on the ground and you have to pick him up. … We’ve got to sit in there and protect him.”

—Las Vegas Raiders tight end Ian Thomas on rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza

Up Next

The 4-6 Raiders hit the road for a Week 11 matchup at the 7-2 Denver Broncos next Sunday. The hard-charging Broncos come off their bye week victors of five-straight games and are tied atop the AFC West with the Kansas City Chiefs. Not only that, but Denver is unbeaten at home this season at 4-0. So the division tilt will be another daunting task for Kubiak, Mendoza, and Co. The Mile High matchup between the two AFC West foes is the first of the divisional two-game tilt and both will face off again in under a month from now.

item.title: Sunday Aftermath: The Chiefs' return, the Patriots' injury misery, and more
item.description: Breaking down all of the NFL's biggest Week 10 storylines, including Patrick Mahomes' monster day against the Falcons.
item.content:encoded:
Is that really all it took? Adding Josh Downs? The Chiefs could have just been adding someone like Josh Downs this entire time? That’s cool, but it’s also exactly what almost literally everyone has been saying for years. Add someone, truly anyone with even baseline pass-catching competency, and this attack could soar again. There just needs to be one other actual receiver to improve the spacing and timing for everyone.

It sounded so simple as to ultimately be unrealistic, naive. “We just don’t know what they know.” It turns out we did. If you give Patrick Mahomes even the 36th best receiver in the NFL opposite, say, the 18th in Rashee Rice, then he could finally get to work again. Maybe this will end up another case of the small-sample size blues vs. a downtrodden and disinterested in Falcons side. We should all be so lucky as to have our one-game sample sizes be five touchdowns and 348 yards passing.

That used to be the norm for Mahomes. It had no longer even been in the range of outcomes since 2023. Now we know it’s back on the menu. It won’t be the most likely result every week, but for games like Week 11 against the Arizona Cardinals? Yeah, I’m thinking Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs are back. If only they added a top-40 wideout sooner.

Five Week 10 Storylines

Emmett Johnson does his best Kenneth Walker III impression in demolition of the Falcons. We knew fifth-round rookie Johnson was not only good, but good enough to earn a plug-and-play RB1 ranking. It turns out we were wrong. He was not a RB1. He was the RB1. Ok, or close to it. Christian McCaffrey and Jahmyr Gibbs still exist. But now we know Johnson does, too. There was nary a touch where Johnson wasn’t either dragging a tackler or avoiding them altogether with the kind of cut-and-juke work usually reserved for, yes, Gibbs. He was powerful in the running game and slippery in the passing attack. We now know he will be an RB1 any time Walker is on the shelf, and we can also hope he can be a more legitimate FLEX even when KWIII is in the lineup. Because, for however nice it is to have Josh Downs, that’s still not really enough. This team needs weapons. They have one in Johnson.

Drake Maye and A.J. Brown both injured in latest Patriots disasterpiece. This one is going to get a lot worse before it gets better. Maye is feared lost for the season. Brown’s season was already lost. It’s over for everybody if Tommy DeVito is forced to start when the Patriots come off bye in Week 12. The only good news is, the collateral damage will be small beyond Maye’s QB1 managers. This Pats season from hell has mustered only the occasional Demario Douglas, Hunter Henry or Mack Hollins spot start “opposite Brown.” Even during Brown’s many absences, true WR3/RB2/FLEX, etc. value has been difficult to come by for the Pats’ ancillary characters. Now we know the whole thing is over. It’s the most bitter of runouts if you bought high on Maye following his dubious MVP runner-up honors, but 2027 will undoubtedly be the perfect time to buy the dip for the young powerhouse.  

Blake Corum has his best game yet as a pro. It felt like Sean McVay had been waiting a long time for the permission to make Corum the centerpiece of his backfield. The Rams' pass catcher injuries finally gave it to him. Freed of the obligation to target anyone in particular through the air, McVay had to base his game plan around the run, where it has become increasingly clear he views Corum as the best choice over Kyren Williams. That was certainly borne out on Sunday, with Corum stuffing the stat sheet and posting far better efficiency marks. This was a one-off game script against a non-competitive Cardinals side. It’s not terribly telling heading into a likely Week 12 shootout with the Packers. But whereas before you had to squint to get Corum into your FLEX spot, that bar has now been shifted to RB2.

Colts’ backfield rotation remains following trade deadline. Playing in one of their last winnable matchups of the season, the Colts did not lean on their best player. Far from it. Taylor handled “just” 67.8 percent of the snaps. Not a bad total, but well off his early-season bell-cow usage. That has now been the case for four consecutive weeks. The previous three came while both sides waited on potential trade developments. The fact that the trend continued following the deadline highlights why Taylor should have been dealt in the first place. The Colts didn’t want Taylor to get hurt ahead of Week 10. Now they don’t want him to get hurt ahead of the offseason, where trade talks should again pick up. They must also evaluate Seth McGowan to know if they can rely on him following any potential move. That, coupled with this deteriorated offensive environment is going to make Taylor more of an unreliable RB2 than locked-in RB1 for the fantasy season’s stretch run.  

Cowboys care more about targeting George Pickens than winning. This is probably an exaggeration, but it certainly felt that way. One owner complaint translated to 18 looks for the No. 2 wideout. Now, we know this is a No. 2 capable of being a No. 1, but when Pickens drew seven targets in the first quarter, you could say the hand was heavy. That it “worked” is besides the point. This is not a team that does the things necessary to win. It has become an all-consuming embarrassment. Pickens, CeeDee Lamb and Dak Prescott are elite players. They do not have an elite coach, or even an ordinary one. They have “Jerry’s guy,” and until that ceases to be the only thing that matters in Dallas, this will remain a laughingstock of an organization that only truly competes on the digital gridiron.

Don't forget, for the latest on everything NFL, check out Rotoworld’s Player News, or follow @Rotoworld_FB or @RotoPat on Twitter/Bluesky.

Five More 10 Storylines

Travis Etienne’s usage makes no more sense in his return. Did the Saints hire Etienne on reference? Had they ever actually seen him play before? Why do they seem like they have zero idea who he is or what he does? So it continued on Sunday, where the highly-compensated Etienne remained a bit player in a three-man committee that has maybe 1.2 actually good running backs at the moment. Neither carrying the mail nor changing the pace, Etienne is just kind of … there. There seems to be no “here” for him to get to, either. We suppose his snaps can only increase after Sunday’s paltry total of 21 — six fewer than scrap heap addition Audric Estime — but it is unclear what the endgame is supposed to be for fantasy players. Were it not for six teams being on bye in Week 11, Etienne would officially be out of lineups. With New Orleans playing and facing the Bears, however, we can place one last ditch second FLEX bet.

Saints fully introduce Jordyn Tyson to the NFL. There was at least one player New Orleans knew what to do with. Of course, it seemed to be the only thing they knew how to do against the Panthers. Tyson went from playing 18 snaps in his Week 9 debut to soaking up all the oxygen in this offense, to the point he out-targeted Chris Olave 13-4. That doesn’t seem terribly smart. Perhaps it was just necessary evaluation during an increasingly lost Saints season, but it was the latest indication this coaching staff has no real plan or vision. React to what’s suddenly in front of you, even if that means pretending one of the best receivers in the NFL in Olave does not exist. That was likely a one-off, but Tyson has firmly implanted himself in the WR3 mix.  

Jets get super, mega banged up in blowout loss. Geno Smith, down. Omar Cooper Jr. hurt yet again, including yet again on the opening series. It’s been that kind of century for Gang Green, but it still doesn’t have to be “that kind of year” for fantasy managers. For as awful as the Jets are, they still have bountiful skill player talent. They also have a backup in Cade Klubnik who appears good enough to at least distribute the ball if Smith is forced to miss time. Smith is the kind of player who rarely misses time, so it could be a moot point. But if/when he is ruled out for Week 11, we can be cautiously optimistic about keeping Garrett Wilson, et al. in our lineups with Klubnik under center. That’s especially true since his “first test” will come vs. a haunted Chargers team playing on a short week.  

Bryce Young’s progress feels like a long, long time ago. Young is back to taking a billion weekly sacks. He’s again routinely completing fewer than 60 percent of his passes. He is struggling to support even one startable fantasy asset in Tetairoa McMillan, let alone two in either Jalen Coker or Darren Waller. He is is again looking completely lost, which is the last thing anyone needed as his rookie contract inches near its conclusion after next season. We don’t really care about that in fantasy, but we do care that Young is giving the Panthers’ coaching staff every reason to draw the shutters for the stretch run. Chuba Hubbard is playing well. Young is not. Where it once appeared we had a priority streamer and multiple other weekly fantasy starters on our hands, we now have merely McMillan, and even him only just.  

There are no winners for the Cardinals’ “left behinds.” I’m not sure what exactly I was expecting, but it still wasn’t that. Zero official targets for waiver wire dart throw Reggie Virgil. No more than three looks for anybody not named Trey McBride. No touches of any kind for the final 12:15 of the game. Yes, the Cardinals allowed the Rams to drain the final 12:15 without even scoring. That is the scale of the Cardinals’ problem. In theory there will be better days ahead for Carson Beck, or at least greater volume after he was limited to 18 attempts against the Rams. In practice, it won’t be Week 11, where the Birds are early three-score underdogs vs. the Chiefs. Abandon all fantasy hope, all ye who enter here.

Questions

1. Not a question, but a statement: If you can't handle me at my Corey Kiner, you don't deserve me at my Emmett Johnson.

2. You don’t know Reggie Virgil’s early stuff? I know the new stuff is lame, but trust me, the old stuff is really good.

3. Did the Saints think Travis Etienne was somebody else? I’m so confused.

Early Waivers Look (Players rostered in less than 50 percent of Yahoo leagues)

It's only the third time this year the Chiefs had a receiver finish with at least 50 yards and a TD in a game (Rashee Rice vs. DEN, Tyquan Thornton vs. LV). Xavier Worthy hasn't gone for 50-plus and a TD since Christmas 2024.”

item.title: Patriots reportedly weighing QB additions despite confidence in Tommy DeVito
item.description: Maye is expected to miss extended time with an ankle injury.
item.content:encoded:
The New England Patriots are expected to be without starting quarterback Drake Maye for an extended period. Maye reportedly suffered a fractured ankle in Germany, an injury that could sideline him for the remainder of the season.

With only Tommy DeVito and rookie Behren Morton on the roster then at quarterback, the Patriots are reportedly expected to explore the market for additional help during their bye week, according to NFL insider Jordan Schultz.

Those options include free agents such as former Patriot Jimmy Garoppolo, who has experience playing under offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels, or signing a quarterback from another team’s practice squad.

Moments before Schultz’s report, head coach Mike Vrabel indicated that he did not currently anticipate the team adding another quarterback.

“I don’t see that being the case right now. But we’ll have conversations and we’ll discuss it and we’ll look and see,” Vrabel said Monday morning. “Tommy and Behren have been in our system and working. Behren’s been improving. Been working each week and I know if he has to play for us that he’ll be ready to go. I’m excited for this challenge and I hope that everybody else is because that’s really what we’re at.”

DeVito struggled after replacing Maye on Sunday, completing just 12-of-24 passes for 81 yards with one touchdown and one interception. The 28-year-old had issues seeing the field and with ball placement.

Vrabel, however, expressed confidence moving forward with DeVito, who the team signed to a two-year extension this offseason to elevate him as Maye’s primary backup.

“The assessment [on DeVito’s performance Sunday] was pretty much like the team, it wasn’t good enough,” Vrabel said. “I think there was some things that he missed. But also not having a ton of live action since training camp, I think he’ll be ready to go coming out of the bye.

“He’ll be ready to look at some things and understand. Whether thats being able to transfer up in the pocket, get us in the right play, or get the ball out quicker, look at protections, rotation, whatever that may all be. I think that’ll all improve. So, I have a lot of confidence in Tommy and I know his toughness will be through the charts, and his competitiveness will be exactly what we need.”

item.title: Packers, Rams embark on shortest possible bye weeks
item.description: In Week 11, six teams will have a bye.
item.content:encoded:
In Week 11, six teams will have a bye. Four will have a full, two-week break. Two will have the shortest possible bye weeks.

It's the latest byproduct of the effort to find more places in the pizza into which cheese can be crammed (and/or from which cash can be siphoned).

The NFL will play its first-ever game on the night before Thanksgiving. The easiest, and more equitable, approach to scheduling entailed giving the Week 12 Wednesday assignment to teams that don't play in Week 11.

Still, it's not a real bye week. The Rams and Packers will play 10 days after their pre-bye games. The usual in-season break is 14 days.

It's possible that a team could play on Monday night and the next Thursday, 10 days later. We're not aware of that happening since the NFL embraced full-season Thursday night games; usually, the league tries to have the same amount of down time for both teams playing on a Thursday night.

Actually, the Packers will get more time off on the back end than the front end of their off week. Green Bay's Week 13 game comes 11 days after the Week 12 game.

The Rams won't be so lucky. They play the Chiefs on the following Thursday night, resulting in 10 days, 8 days, and 10 days between L.A. games.

But that's how it will go in the new and improved NFL. More windows. More prime-time games. More international games.

All with the objective of the ultimate more.

More money.

item.title: Fantasy Football: Target share for Justin Jefferson with Kirk Cousins back, plus more key stats from Week 10
item.description: Joel Smyth takes you through some key stats from Week 10 that should help with fantasy football going forward.
item.content:encoded:
In fantasy football, you have to look back to move forward. Fantasy points are the goal, but how a player gets there is the key. Analyst Joel Smyth breaks down 8 numbers to know from Week 10 in order to win your matchup in Week 11 and beyond.

28

Touches for Emmett Johnson in Week 10, the fourth-most on the week. Johnson took full advantage of Kenneth Walker III being absent for the week, taking on 22 of the 24 RB carries and all seven of the RB targets. The rookie became a 1:1 replacement and a week winner for those who picked him up this weekend. He should be kept no matter the availability of Walker in Week 11, and can even be used as a flex next weekend, with Walker likely being limited against a Cardinals defense that will be significant underdogs in Kansas City.

This should be a wake-up call for the importance of fantasy insurance RBs late in the season. Bye weeks are largely behind us, the waivers are shrinking and the upside for top RB2s is clear. It was very well known that if Walker was out of the picture, even for a game, Johnson would become the favorite for workhorse volume. The rate of late-round running backs posting RB1 numbers doubles over the last month of the season, making now the next best time to pick one up for your bench.

5-8

Targets and routes for Josh Downs in his first game as a Kansas City Chief. It’s a new day for the young WR, going from a struggling offense led by Daniel Jones to an immediate season-high performance on eight routes with Patrick Mahomes. Downs was not only the go-to guy when on the field, but also capitalized on his opportunities with four receptions, 53 yards and a touchdown.

The Chiefs brought in Downs to help as a desperately needed man-coverage beater, but also as a downfield target so far. Three of Downs’ five targets were 10+ yards downfield, tying a team high in such targets out of the gate, catching all three. Rashee Rice will get a lot of the work around the line of scrimmage while Downs can continue to help Mahomes push the ball downfield after starting dead last in air yards per attempt. That usage wasn’t working with Jones in Indianapolis; however, the QB upgrade often fixes that.

15.6%

Targets per route for Chris Olave the last two weeks when Jordyn Tyson has been on the field. Before Tyson’s return, his 25.9% targets per route was one of the best in the NFL, leading him to WR1 numbers. The two-week sample becomes more dangerous in my eyes with it not being just okay production, but dominant target volume in a WR’s first two career games. This offense has been perfect for Olave because of the volume, rather than being a top-10 offense. Tyson being targeted on 38% of routes so far is a major problem, not that it will stay that extreme, but that his routes are still limited.

The Saints will have weeks where their high-volume passing attack will be enough to satisfy both, but there will be more days where Olave isn’t saved by top-five WR volume as the Saints’ offense struggles as a whole.

WR with 10+ receptions in a game within their first 2 games since 2020

2026 Jordyn Tyson
2024 Malik Nabers
2023 Puka Nacua pic.twitter.com/Ti7XPxM5nd

— PFF (@PFF) November 15, 2026

33%

Snaps for Travis Etienne Jr. in his return. The playing time can certainly increase, but the three-RB committee looks strong and much tougher to overcome than simply one RB. Audric Estime still played a major role, leading the backfield with 27 snaps. Kamara was third, but did have four of the six red-zone snaps, and Etienne at least led in touches (11).  Even worse than the volume issue is the efficiency issue. The Panthers entered 31st against RBs, it can’t get much better. The Saints helped that ranking improve on Sunday with 17 carries for 24 rushing yards. They had negative yards before contact, zero carries over five yards and combined for 59 scrimmage yards. Although the schedule will have some bright spots, the New Orleans backfield is likely to continue to be messy, splitting three ways in an offense that ranks 27th in rushing yards per game. ​

43%

Target share for Justin Jefferson in his first game with Kirk Cousins this season. Jefferson benefitted from T.J. Hockenson and Jordan Addison being unavailable, but almost everything else was positive for future outlook. His 13 targets and nine receptions were immediate season highs, with Minnesota having its second-highest scoring game on the season, resulting in an expected 23.9 fantasy points, the fourth-highest on the week. The production as a team was there and should show up stronger in the fantasy box score soon. In terms of fit, it was a great start to the change.

Cousins loves to target receivers on in-breaking routes and over the middle of the field compared to Kyler Murray, and that showed immediately. Jefferson was targeted five times over the middle of the field, over twice as much as his average to begin the year, an area of his game that has lost the most value since Sam Darnold left town. The beginning of Cousins saving this offense and Jefferson’s fantasy season look promising.

60%

Of the Colts RB touches went to Jonathan Taylor on Sunday, lower than it’s been on average the last few weeks. Not according to plan! What was expected was that now that the Colts have no reason to save Taylor, and they don’t have a first-round pick to tank for, their star RB would go back to getting 85%+ of the workload. Seth McGowan thought otherwise. The RB split in Indianapolis stayed nearly the exact same as the previous few weeks, resulting in Taylor being vulture-picked in the red zone and posting a very modest fantasy performance given the opponent. This was Taylor’s best opportunity the rest of the season, and was largely wasted without the high-end RB volume we’re used to seeing. He’s talented enough to overcome low volume, or a low offense, but not many can do both. A road matchup versus a Texans’ run defense on Thursday Night Football will be a much more difficult task at hand.

5

Targets for Trey McBride on Carson Beck’s 18 passing attempts Sunday, his lowest in a game since 2024. The worry wasn’t necessarily that Beck wouldn’t target McBride as often, but that a high target share wouldn’t equal high targets. McBride’s 28% target share is pretty normal for the fantasy superstar; it just doesn’t work on only 34 offensive plays with 11 completions. The Cardinals aren’t just on their third-string QB, but their WR5 is the new WR1, their offensive line is banged up, their top-five drafted RB is on IR and it’s showing on the scoreboard. After taking five sacks, Beck only completed a pass on 45% of his dropbacks, much below Jacoby Brissett’s 58%, or even Gardner Minshew’s No. 1 rate in a small sample. The volume will come back at times when the offense can sustain more drives, but it’s just the start of the issues, with scoring upside and receiving efficiency also raising concerns.

41-16

The snap differential between Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price in Week 10, favoring Charbonnet. After a 50-50 split the last two weeks, the veteran made a real leap over the rookie, resulting in 2x as many touches (20-10). When Price was on the field, he was very involved in the offense, touching the ball on 10 of his 15 snaps; it’s just hard to get much more when you’re barely on the field. The Seahawks relied on Charbonnet in the passing game, running 15 routes versus Price’s six, and turned their first-round pick into a worse version of 2025 Kenneth Walker III. Yes, he got the TD, but the score only resulted in 10.9 points and modest hope for future volume. Price has averaged under 10 fantasy PPG since returning, with the worst part being that it was versus a very friendly schedule. Upcoming, the Seahawks have the bye week before San Francisco, the No. 2 team against rushing fantasy points.

item.title: Mike Vrabel on Drake Maye: I wouldn't imagine him being available out of the bye
item.description: There has been mixed reporting about the status of Drake Maye's ankle injury after the Patriots lost to the Lions in Munich on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
There has been mixed reporting about the status of Drake Maye's ankle injury after the Patriots lost to the Lions in Munich on Sunday.

New England will be on its bye in Week 11. In his Monday press conference, head coach Mike Vrabel would only go as far as noting the quarterback's likely status for Week 12.

“I’m not going to make any comments about his status until he gets back here,” Vrabel said. “He’s en route back here. He stayed with a few of our people and they’re en route back here. So, once he gets back here, our people are able to visit with him again, talk with him again, I think we’ll have more to offer.

“But I wouldn’t imagine him being available when we come out of the bye.”

PFT reported on Sunday night that Maye is expected to be out for a while, with others reporting on Monday that the quarterback may not be back at all in 2026.

But Vrabel said at this point, he doesn’t expect the team to go and sign another quarterback. Tommy DeVito and and Behren Morton are the other QBs on the 53-man roster. The team does not have a quarterback on the practice squad.

item.title: Dolphins waive kicker Zane Gonzalez
item.description: Miami gives struggling kicker the boot after Sunday’s three-miss performance.
item.content:encoded:
The Miami Dolphins have waived kicker Zane Gonzalez.

File this under the “least surprising news of the day” category.

After a miserable game on Sunday against the Indianapolis Colts that saw Miami’s former kicker miss two field goals and an extra point try in a tilt that the Dolphins lost by just two points, general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan gave Gonzalez his walking papers early on Monday.

In his four games with the Dolphins, Gonzalez went 6 for 10 on field goal tries, and 6 for 7 on extra point tries — missing 5 total kicks since he replaced Riley Patterson in South Florida.

Last week, the Dolphins hosted two kickers for tryouts — Daniel Carlson and Ben Sauls. Sauls has played in just three games during his short NFL career, but went 8 for 8 as a member of the New York Giants last season. Carlson — a 9 year veteran — has a career field goal percentage of 86%, going 233 for 271 while playing for multiple teams including the Las Vegas Raiders and New Orleans Saints. However, Carlson was released by New Orleans earlier this season after going just 8 for 12 in field goal attempts in 7 games played.

We will continue to keep you updated on all things Miami Dolphins as the team prepares for a matchup against the Buffalo Bills this coming Sunday.

item.title: 9 Winners, 7 losers, and 1 IDK from the 49ers win over the Cowboys
item.description: A review from everything we saw in the 49ers-Cowboys game
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers and Dallas Cowboys came close to reaching 100 points in Week 10. It was a game where defense was optional. The offenses had their way. Big plays were the norm, and two of the league’s most potent offenses didn’t disappoint.

Let’s get into the Winners and Losers from Week 10.

Winners

Brock Purdy

We try to stay away from listing core players in this section. Even Purdy’s biggest naysayers can’t use this performance or “it’s the Cowboys’ defense” against him.

Purdy led all quarterbacks in Week 10 with a 0.77 EPA per pass. Second-place Matthew Stafford was 0.63. Purdy had the second-highest passing success rate at 63.6%. He completed nearly 80% of his passes and threw for three touchdowns. Sprinkle in a couple of much-needed scrambles, and it was your typical ho-hum performance from Purdy this season.

Five sacks may be alarming — you could argue only one was on the offensive line — but those were offset by 3 completions of 20+ yards in the air. A couple of improv plays off-script where Purdy manipulated the pocket around him, made unblocked defenders miss, and created first downs (one was a touchdown) when nothing was there.

There’s more evidence that shows Purdy’s excellence from Sunday. The offense averaged 0.48 EPA per play, the highest of any offense this season.

Purdy sliced and diced the Cowboys against man coverage. He completed 12 of 16 passes against man coverage for 273 yards and three touchdowns. That was the most yards in a game facing man coverage by any player since 2021. When Purdy scrambled, he was 4-for-4 for 135 yards and a touchdown. That number ties Patrick Mahomes (W4 2018) and Josh Allen (W15 2024) for the most scramble passing yards in a game since 2018. Against the blitz, Purdy went 6-for-6 for 197 yards and two scores.

Christian McCaffrey

McCaffrey topped 20 mph on his 66-yard touchdown. He did a fantastic job making himself available and getting into Purdy’s line of sight on the 74-yard touchdown.

Surprisingly, McCaffrey had a rushing success rate of only 23.1%. But he made several impact plays on those carries, gained 35 yards after contact, forced two missed tackles, and had two 10+ yard runs, including a 16-yard touchdown.

CMC is here because of his work through the air. He had a third-down target where he beat Caleb Downs for a much-needed first down. McCaffrey came through in the clutch when the offense needed a big play.

McCaffrey became the first running back in NFL history with multiple 65+ yard touchdown receptions in the same game. He had the most receiving yards by a running back since Jamaal Charles’s 195 yards in Week 15 of 2013.

Kaelon Black

Welcome to the show, rook.

Black forced three missed tackles — two of them on one play. He had 53 rush yards, 44 of which came after contact. Again, the success rate was below average (27.3%), but the big plays more than make up for it. Black contributed 13 yards through the air, but he’s here for running over a first-down and finishing in the end zone.

Deebo Samuel

Deebo had a 70-yard touchdown on a play where Cowboys defenders didn’t figure out he had the ball until he was 20 yards downfield. Samuel had two other carries for four yards. He caught a screen for a touchdown. He had two other catches for 20 yards. He was efficient, effective, and electric. Samuel ran just under 20 miles per hour on his touchdown run.

Keenan Allen

I’d argue that Allen helped get the offense off the mat. The player who wasn’t on the roster this time last week had the second-most targets. Allen caught five passes for 61 yards. He had a 25% target share — which is Mike Evans territory.

Four of Allen’s receptions resulted in a first down, and he should’ve had five if Purdy didn’t miss him toward the end of the game.

We expected Allen to be impactful underneath, but he showed that he can create separation at the intermediate level of the field, both on in- and out-breaking routes.

Jordan Watkins

Watkins kicked things off with a 22-yard reception. He had a 27-yarder where Purdy bought time, waiting for someone to get open, while Watkins picked himself up off the ground and made himself available. It was only two catches, but Watkins has proven to be a big-play threat.

Watkins had a couple of blocks that helped spring plays for the offense. He’s developing nicely and rounding into a complete player.

George Kittle

Kittle had a 20+ yard screen pass. He had four first-down receptions on nine targets. Every time he touched the ball, it felt like an impact play. Kittle caught three of his four contested targets, something he struggled with over the past couple of games. He had 46 yards after the catch. It wasn’t a vintage Kittle day, but if 74 yards feels like an off day, you know you’re dealing with a star.

Losers

Connor Colby

Of the 115 offensive linemen to play at least 50 snaps in Week 10, Colby ranked 112th with a 17.1% pressure rate allowed. He had six pressures. Usually, Colby makes up for it in the run game. That was not the case on Sunday. You try to give the seventh-rounder some grace, especially going against Quinnen Williams. But you have to be competitive, and Colby simply was not. His lows are in the basement, and teams will start going out of their way to stress Colby.

Deommodore Lenoir

Lenoir was targeted 17 times against Dallas. That is not a typo. Over half of those came in the first half. That’s the third-most targets for a cornerback in a game since 2022.

Coming into the game, Renardo Green was up against CeeDee Lamb, and Lenoir was up against George Pickens. On the surface, it makes sense. Put your better corner on their best receiver, and try to minimize the damage.

Lenoir broke up the first two passes his way on the first drive, and you thought, ‘OK, he’s confident, and will hold his own.‘ Dallas completed the next five passes his way. We’ll talk ad nauseam about the pass rush, but the coverage was worse, and Lenoir is leading the charge.

It’s 46-32. 1:56 remains. Keion White beats his man cleanly. Dak Prescott gets hit at the top of his drop. Lenoir allows an 11-yard curl to Pickens. First down.

Far too many occurrences where there was pressure, but the coverage wasn’t in a position to contest the throw. Despite all those targets, Lenoir forced tight-window throws only 25% of the time. That’s not competitive. You don’t have a chance to survive.

Interior line play

The Cowboys ran 76 plays. Let’s add some context to the poor play. The defensive line was clearly gassed and running on fumes. With that said, the interior was getting pushed around in the first half, and fortunate Dallas didn’t run the ball on them more.

Osa Odighizuwa had three run stops and four pressures. That’s about as well as he can play. DeForest Buckner had three pressures. Sebastian Valdez had two, and James Thompson had one. Pass-rush win rate is a better indicator of how a player performed. Only Odighizuwa was in the double digits. Buckner, who played 55 snaps and 39 pass-rushing snaps, only won on 5.1% of his rushes. He has to be better.

Epeshians Prysock

A tough spot for a rookie to get extended action. Prysock went in for Renardo Green after Green left with a back injury. Prysock played 28 snaps. He allowed all three of his targets to be completed for 28 yards, including a touchdown. He also missed a tackle. Prysock didn’t need to grab the receiver in the end zone, since he was already in position. That penalty nearly cost the Niners the game.

Penalties

The 49ers have been sloppy for three weeks now, and the penalties are starting to add up. They had 11 against Dallas, giving the Cowboys a full football field (100 yards) of penalties. The Cowboys had four first downs from penalties.

The operation was smooth for the first month and a half of the season, but the Niners have been trending in the wrong direction with the zebras.

The refs

Bring on the robots. It’s time. Malik Mustapha had a picture-perfect hit. The refs huddled up, talked it over, and still decided Mustapha made illegal contact. Why couldn’t replay assist chime in?

I counted at least four times when George Kittle fought through illegal contact during a route. There was an obvious penalty on a third-down target that wasn’t called. You don’t expect perfection from the refs, but some of the calls and non-calls in this game were egregious.

Late-down defense

If you break up the 49ers into late and early downs, it’s a tale of two games. The Cowboys were in the 56th percentile running the ball on early downs, compared to the 100th percentile on late downs.

Forcing the Cowboys into 21 late-down conversions is a sign that you’re doing your job on early downs. But Dallas converted 11 of those, including 4-of-5 on fourth down.

It was a unique challenge, and only two or three other teams can attack the Niners the way Dallas did, but it’s still no excuse to allow as many plays or give up as many late-down conversions as the Niners did.

IDKs

The pass rush

Again, 76 plays. Dallas had drives of 8, 11, 7, 7, 8, 10, and 12. Good things do not happen when you’re on the field that often.

We touched on Odighizuwa’s production. The edge-rushing group won, and they did so far more than most fans are willing to admit. Remember, coming into this game, Prescott was the fifth-least-sacked quarterback in the NFL. Last week, Kirk Cousins was second. Context is key when we’re talking about sacks.

Among the edge rushers who played at least 50 snaps in Week 10, Nick Bosa ranked third in pass-rush win rate at 15.8%. Bosa had five pressures and would’ve forced a turnover had Dre Greenlaw caught the ball. That removes one score off the board.

I mentioned the Keion White QB hit on third down when Lenoir wasn’t in position. The Niners hit Prescott 10 times. That’s in the 95th percentile.

Filtering it down to at least 25 pass-rush snaps, White was 19th in pass-rush win rate, and Mykel Williams was 21st. That’s three players in the top 21. Mykel had a sack that was negated by a penalty (on Lenoir, of course), and that led to points.

That’s three plays where you’re taking three scoring drives off the board. We’d be having a much different conversation about the pass rush if the secondary didn’t make a mistake. But it’s a results-based business, and there were no sacks, so it’s understandable why there’s an uproar. Still, you have to ignore a ton of data to think the Niners didn’t get after Prescott in Week 10. That’s not accurate.

Winners

Renardo Green

Green matched up against Lamb and limited him to 23 yards on three catches. He held Pickens to 14 yards on three targets. Renardo also broke up a pass. It was a nice bounce-back for Green, who didn’t back down from the challenge the Cowboys presented.

Malik Mustapha

Mustapha played 59 snaps, which led the way for the three-man rotation. Ji’Ayir Brown played 57, while Marques Sigle played 44. The rotation needs to end. Not saying it would have made a difference, but Dallas scored when Mustapha wasn’t on the field.

They targeted Mustapha four times, and he broke up two passes and intercepted another. He did have a penalty and missed a tackle, but it’s clear to anyone with eyes that he’s one of the only reliable players in the secondary. In my mind, he’s closer to a Pro Bowl starter than an average one.

item.content:encoded:
The Cowboys may be without right guard Tyler Booker in the coming weeks.

Booker left Sunday's 46-40 loss to the 49ers after playing 33 offensive snaps and Ian Rapoport of NFL Media reports that he is dealing with a high-ankle sprain.

High-ankle sprains often lead to multi-week absences and Booker missed three games with a similar injury last season. The Cowboys face the Titans, Eagles and Seahawks before a bye in Week 14.

T.J. Bass took over for the final 50 snaps of Sunday's loss and will likely be at right guard until Booker is cleared to return to action.

item.title: Aaron Glenn had DC Brian Duker calling Jets defensive plays on Sunday
item.description: The Jets's eighth loss of the 2026 season had things in common with the previous seven, but Sunday's outing against the Bills was different in one significant way.
item.content:encoded:
The Jets's eighth loss of the 2026 season had things in common with the previous seven, but Sunday's outing against the Bills was different in one significant way.

Head coach Aaron Glenn confirmed at a Monday press conference that he had defensive coordinator Brian Duker calling the defensive plays for the first time this season.

"I gave Duker the lead when it comes to that. I’m still a huge part of what we call," Glenn said.

Glenn said last week that he was "looking at everything" when it came to finding ways for the Jets to improve on their 2-7 start and reiterated on Monday that he is willing to do "anything that I can do as a head coach to help us win games." The Jets gave up 389 yards in the 31-12 loss to the Bills, including 201 rushing yards that included a 74-yard James Cook touchdown run late in the fourth quarter.

Duker's predecessor Steve Wilks was Glenn's initial defensive playcaller in 2025, but he was fired in mid-December and Glenn announced he would take over that responsibility in the offseason. Glenn had called the plays as the Lions' defensive coordinator and called that his "superpower" in February, but opposing offenses have proven to be his kryptonite far too often during the 2026 season.

item.content:encoded:
The Dolphins are looking for a new kicker.

item.title: The Morning After: The Steelers have reason to worry, but not to panic
item.description: The Steelers have reason to be concerned, but a lot of wins remain on the table.
item.content:encoded:
Yes, but also no. That is my final answer to a question we’ll get to in a bit.

My fandom of the Pittsburgh Steelers can be traced back to 2004. I don’t know why I said “traced back” like an archeologist who is figuring out where a specific dinosaur bone came from, but that is the earliest memory I have of being a fan. In my now 22 years of watching football, Sunday night was pound-for-pound the worst performance I’ve ever seen out of a Steelers team.

Where do you want to start with how outmatched the Steelers were? How about 484 yards to 222 in favor of the Bengals? Or Ja’Marr Chase having more receiving yards (231) than the Steelers did yards of offense. Quarterback wise, Joe Burrow had more passing yards in the first half than Aaron Rodgers has had in any game in his tenure as the Steelers’ quarterback. I could keep going – and I will. Rodgers’ 143 yards passing are the third-fewest he’s thrown in a full game as a Steeler. However, 118 of those came in the fourth quarter during garbage time. So if you took away those last two meaningless drives, Rodgers was 8-of-20 for 25 yards. The defense had by far its worse game of the season, as well, allowing Joe Burrow to put up the third-highest total EPA of any quarterback in any game this season, behind only to Drake Maye in Week 5 against the Las Vegas Raiders and Brock Purdy on Sunday against the Dallas Cowboys.

That brings me back to the teased question, which is should the Steelers be panicked? After any game like that, yes there should be more concern than not. Constant defensive miscommunications, Asante Samuel’s inability to look like an NFL caliber player when lined up agains top tier receivers, blitzes being dissected like nothing, an inability to get any pressure on Burrow, and a passing game that is completely dead in the water – those are all massive, massive concerns.

So if those are all real, major issues, what is the case for taking a deep breath and not proclaiming the season to be over? Well, the remaining schedule is much more favorable than we originally thought. Next week, they’ll play the Joe Milton-led Philadelphia Eagles, who haven’t scored more than 20 points just twice this season – that’s a game they should absolutely win. They then host the Broncos, whose defense is incredible, but offensively, they are brutal. Denver is 28th in offensive success rate and 25th in passing yards per game. At home, the Steelers can beat Bo Nix and make life hell for the Broncos’ less-than-stellar offense. They then face a Texans team that is currently 3-6 and allowed the Browns to come back from a 17-0 hole to win. On the road against the Jaguars will be tough, and I don’t expect them to beat the most complete team in the AFC. But then they have a home game against the Panthers – should be a win – followed by a road game against the Titans – should be a win. Those games are sandwiched between both tilts against the Ravens in Weeks 15 and 18, both of which are likely to not feature Lamar Jackson, especially if the Ravens are mathematically eliminated from playoff contention.

Is this all to say the Steelers are Super Bowl contenders? No, and I’m not going to gaslight you by saying they are. And if in your eyes that means that everything else isn’t worth talking about, then I don’t know what you’re doing here, frankly. A team is never as great as their greatest highs or as bad as their lowest lows. The Steelers are still a 6-3 team with seven very winnable games remaining on their schedule, and a Jaguars game that I don’t expect them to win, but you never know what can happen any given week. 12 wins is still very much on the table, 11 even more so, and 10 at the absolute worst. I can already see some of you pounding at the keyboard. “THEY AREN’T WINNING ANOTHER GAME THIS SEASON.”

Relax.

The Steelers find themselves at a crossroads, not a dead end. Was it an awful performance? Absolutely. Is that the norm this team has put on display this season? Absolutely not. Hell, the 2020 Buccaneers were blown out 38-3 on Sunday Night Football and they won the Super Bowl. Performances like this happen to every good-great team each season to varying degrees. The Steelers are still going to be a playoff team. What happens after that, we can be angry about if and when it goes south when the time comes. For now, deep breaths.

Let us know what you think in the comments. Be sure to bookmark Behind the Steel Curtain for all the latest news, breakdowns, and more!
