item.title: Patrick Mahomes strengthened his all-time legacy in Week 10
item.description: Kansas City’s favorite quarterback continues etching his name into the NFL’s record books.
item.content:encoded:
It was a prolific performance by Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes in the 35-13 win over the Atlanta Falcons in Week 10. He threw for 348 yards and five touchdowns, firing downfield with authority like it was 2018.

He has been writing his name into the NFL’s all-time record books since that first year as a starter, taking home the MVP, but this vintage game etched Mahomes further into them.

Including the postseason, Mahomes now has 332 career touchdown passes, which surpassed Pro Football Hall of Famer Peyton Manning (327) for the most touchdown passes by a quarterback in their first 10 seasons. Of course, Mahomes started just one game in his first year, making the accolade all the more impressive.

The five-touchdown performance in Atlanta — the seventh of his career — also put him in elite company, making him just the fourth quarterback ever to hit the mark that many times.

  • Mahomes (7)
  • Peyton Manning (9)
  • Tom Brady (9)
  • Drew Brees (11)

Of course, Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen made history himself on Sunday by scoring the most total touchdowns (323) over the first 10 regular seasons of an NFL player’s career, passing Manning despite playing in just his ninth season this year.

But when it comes to passing touchdowns, Mahomes has stacked them up in bunches more than anybody. He is now the first player in NFL history with at least three touchdown passes in 50 games within the first 10 seasons of his career. He’s also the first quarterback to have 20 games with four or more touchdown passes in that span.

Chiefs Kingdom doesn’t usually need reminding that their favorite quarterback is one of the league’s all-time greats, but the numbers keep making that case for Mahomes.

item.title: 5 NFL players who have hurt themselves celebrating, now including Aidan Hutchinson
item.description: This is the worst list to be on.
item.content:encoded:
The most devastating play of the 2026 NFL season unspooled in Munich, Germany when Detroit Lions star Aidan Hutchinson turned the corner and chased down New England Patriots star Drake Maye during the first quarter of a Week 10 showdown. Maye suffered a “significant lower leg” injury on the play. Hutchinson was just fine … until he started his celebration.

Hutchinson ran a few yards and leapt in the air to celebrate his sixth sack of the season. When he came down, he had torn his ACL in his right knee. It’s a crushing loss for a Lions team that would be the No. 2 seed in the NFC if the NFL Playoffs started today. This is extremely hard to watch now knowing the aftermath of the play.

In the process, Hutchinson joined a dubious list of football players who have been injured while celebrating, and many of them have had disastrous consequences.

Hutchinson’s injury was eerily similar to another torn ACL suffered after sacking a New England Patriots quarterback. Back in 2014, Chicago Bears EDGE rusher Lamarr Houston went down with the same injury after celebrating a sack while his team was already down 25 points in the fourth quarter.

Another infamous moment that came to mind was Bill Gramatica’s ACL injury. In 2001, Gramatica was a kicker for the Arizona Cardinals who tore his ACL celebrating a 42-yard field goal against the New York Giants.

This still hurts to watch:

How can we forget Gus Frerotte giving himself a concussion after celebrating a touchdown run by headbutting a padded concrete wall? Yikes.

The Lions had another defensive lineman go down on a very similar play to Hutchinson about 12 years earlier. Stephen Tulloch tried to taunt Aaron Rodgers by mimicking the QB’s “discount double check” celebration back in 2014. Trying to copy Rodgers’ gimmick cost him a torn ACL.

Hutchinson is clearly the best player on this list. His injury brings to mind Dan Campbell’s famous line after Detroit lost in January 2024 following the 2023 season.

“I told those guys, this may have been our only shot,” Campbell said.

Since then, the Lions have survived the loss of both coordinators to remain an elite team in the NFC. Now they need to persevere again to overcome the loss of arguably their best defensive player. Hutchinson’s injury should be a lesson for future generations so history doesn’t repeat itself: play it cool after a big moment. You don’t want to be next on this list.

item.title: Panthers on pace to set new NFL records for most penalties and penalty yards this season
item.description: The Panthers beat the Saints on Sunday despite being assessed a whopping 17 penalties for 152 yards.
item.content:encoded:
The Panthers beat the Saints on Sunday despite being assessed a whopping 17 penalties for 152 yards. If they keep it up, they're going to end this season with more penalties and more penalty yards than any team has ever had.

Through nine games, the Panthers lead the NFL with 87 penalties for 787 yards. That puts them on pace for 164 penalties for 1,487 yards in 17 games, both of which would be new NFL records. The current NFL records were set by the 2011 Oakland Raiders, who were assessed 163 penalties for 1,358 yards.

Panthers coach Dave Canales said after Sunday's game that he can accept some penalties that are naturally going to happen over the course of a game, but he doesn't accept mental mistakes like jumping offside.

"Some of the penalties that are judgment calls, they're gonna call them how they see them," Canales said. "The things that I'm gonna focus on are the ones we have to take control of, which are offside penalties, pre-snap, delay of games, those type of procedural penalties. We've got to eliminate those. The competitive calls are going to happen. There's ways to talk about the technique, but it's really the things that we can control that we have to focus on."

Asked if he had a problem with the officials on Sunday, who assessed the Saints just three penalties while the Panthers got 17, Canales answered, "I'm not gonna get into that."

Canales did address the penalties with his team, however.

"We talked about the penalties. We set a new franchise record with 17, and we have to fix that. That's not gonna be sustainable in this league, when the margins are so tight. The guys understand that," Canales said.

What Canales will do is address what his own team can do better, perhaps improving enough over the second half of the season to avoid breaking a record that no coach wants to break.

item.title: Fantasy Football Waiver Wire Week 11: Add Emari Demercado and Adonai Mitchell
item.description: With Omar Cooper Jr. banged up, Adonai Mitchell is poised for a strong close to the fantasy regular season. Emari Demercado is taking over in Houston, putting him on FLEX radar as well.
item.content:encoded:
Week 10 is nearly in the books and the fantasy playoffs are in sight. These are the biggest waiver wire adds as we push toward the fantasy football postseason.

Week 10 Stock Up, Stock Down: Mayeday
Rivers McCown highlights four fantasy players whose fantasy football stock rose in Week 10 of the NFL season and four whose stock fell.
  • Rivers McCown,

▶ Quarterback

J.J. McCarthy, Giants

While not perfect, McCarthy played another solid game on Thursday night, throwing for 293 yards and a touchdown. He’s currently 15th in EPA per dropback and 10th in completion percent over expected on the season (min. 100 dropbacks). McCarthy is also tied with Lamar Jackson for the highest aDOT (10.4) among qualified quarterbacks. He’s an aggressive downfield thrower who also brings something to the table with his legs. McCarthy and the Giants get a potential shootout with the Jags next week.

Cam Ward, Titans

Ward is coming off his two best fantasy outings of the season. He threw a pair of touchdowns in Week 10 and in Week 8 before the team’s bye. Over the past month, Ward ranks 13th in EPA per play and 10th in CPOE. Now he gets a date with a Dallas defense that has been a money-printing machine for opposing offenses.

Aaron Rodgers, Steelers

Rodgers bailed fantasy managers out from a truly awful performance with a pair of garbage time touchdowns on Sunday night. His production has taken a nosedive over the past three weeks with 527 yards and three touchdowns in total. On the other hand, Rodgers has a get-right spot on tap versus the Eagles. Philly is 23rd in EPA per dropback allowed. They have given up the ninth-most fantasy points to opposing QBs.

▶ Running Back

Emari Demercado, Texans

David Montgomery hasn’t played in over a month because of a groin issue. With a Thursday game on deck for Houston, he may be held out another week, though we’ll get more information via the team’s upcoming practice reports. Woody Marks suffered a concussion in Week 10 and did not return. He’s unlikely to clear the league’s protocol ahead of Thursday. Demercado saw seven carries in Week 10 and Dare Ogunbowale only saw one. Demercado also out-targeted him 2-1. If you’re desperate for one week of RB3 production, Demercado is worth a 15-20 percent FAAB bid.

Kaleb Johnson, Packers

Johnson took over for Josh Jacobs in Week 10. The fantasy results weren’t there, but the role was okay. He out-carried MarShawn Lloyd and Chris Brooks combined 10-6. Johnson easily leads the Packers in yards after contact per attempt at 3.6. No one else is over 2.3. He’s also the only Packer with more than one carry of 15+ yards. Johnson should be Green Bay’s lead back until Jacobs returns.

Seth McGowan, Colts

The Colts are throttling down Jonathan Taylor’s usage in a lost year. He ran the ball 16 times on Sunday, but McGowan saw a dozen carries and punched in a goal line touchdown. McGowan has 36 touches and two touchdowns over the past month. He’s on the RB3/4 border and holds immense contingent value should Taylor get banged up.

Kaelon Black, 49ers

It’s a similar story for Black, who has double-digit carries in three straight games. He found the end zone versus Dallas on Sunday, giving him two touchdowns in his past three appearances. Black has played well this year, averaging 4.5 YPC and 3.0 yards after contact per attempt. He’s a touchdown-or-bust RB3 who might be the most valuable backup in all of fantasy.

Austin Ekeler, Commanders

Ekeler has forced a full-blown committee in Washington. He saw nine carries to Rachaad White’s 11 on Thursday. Both backs ran 14 routes, but Ekeler earned four targets to White’s two. Ekeler has a more fantasy-friendly role than McGowan and Black because of his receiving production, but he also holds very little contingent value. His role will shrink when Jacory Croskey-Merritt returns, which could happen this week, so I wouldn’t spend more than a few FAAB dollars on him.

Jonathon Brooks, Panthers

Brooks returned to practice last week but did not play in Sunday’s game. He has been on IR for most of the season with a groin injury that initially surfaced late in training camp. Chuba Hubbard has played extremely well as the Panthers’ workhorse this year, and I don’t expect Brooks to threaten him for the RB1 role. He could, however, provide a much-needed change of pace for Hubbard, who is currently sixth in the NFL in touches. Brooks is an interesting deep league stash but nothing more.

▶ Wide Receiver

Adonai Mitchell, Jets

Omar Cooper Jr. injured his ankle for a third time in Week 10. He will likely miss multiple weeks to let the issue fully heal. That narrows the target tree in New York to just two players: Garrett Wilson and Mitchell. The latter saw eight targets and 118 air yards on Sunday, though he posted another quiet box score. Mitchell is up to 478 air yards over his past three appearances. The production will be highly unpredictable, but Mitchell is worth spending 10-15 percent of your FAAB on if you still have the firepower.

Ryan Flournoy, Cowboys

Flournoy opened the season with a relatively quiet month of football. He’s been quietly productive ever since. He’s averaging 4.2 catches for 60 yards and .5 touchdowns in his past six games. That’s 13.2 PPR points per week. Dallas gets a low-wattage matchup versus the Titans this week, but Flournoy is at least in the FLEX mix.

Elic Ayomanor, Titans

Ayomanor took over Carnell Tate’s role as the Titans’ lead receiver in Week 10. He amassed 10 targets, good for a 26 percent target share, and caught five balls for 79 yards. Ayomanor was also taken down inside the five-yard line, preventing him from a true breakout game. He’s only on the fantasy radar if Tate is out for Week 11, but a date with Dallas sans Tate would put him in the WR3 mix.

Claeb Douglas, Dolphins

A trick play allowed Malik Washington and Jalen Tolbert to out-score Douglas this week, but the rookie is pulling away as Miami’s clear WR1. He led the team with eight targets and a 24 percent air yards share. Douglas also tallied 154 air yards, which easily led the Dolphins. Kyle McCord repeatedly pushed the ball downfield, even if his success rate on those throws wasn’t particularly good. He did just enough on Sunday to keep the light on for a Douglas WR3 candidacy.

Xavier Hutchinson, Texans

Nico Collins finally returned to form with a 9/94/1 line on Sunday. Hutchinson, however, emerged as the Texans’ clear No. 2 receiver, seeing nine targets and a 24 percent target share. The Texans have always trusted Hutchinson to run the WR2 routes in the offense, even if his efficiency has left a lot to be desired. The acquisition of Marvin Harrison Jr. briefly put an end to that, but he’s now injured, meaning the No. 2 job is up for grabs again. Hutchinson will be worth a flyer for as long as MHJ remains out.

▶ Tight End

Chig Okonkwo, Commanders

Okonkwo watched on as Ben Sinnott scored in Week 10, but he remained one of Jayden Daniels’ favorite targets. Okonkwo earned eight opportunities through the air, second only to Stefon Diggs. He has at least six targets in four of his past five games. There isn’t much ceiling with Chig, but he has developed a solid TE2 floor headed into Week 11.

Gavin Bartholomew, Vikings

Bartholomew took over for an injured T.J. Hockenson this week and acquitted himself well. He ran a route on 67 percent of Kirk Cousins’ dropbacks and earned a 13 percent target share. Neither number is great, but Bartholomew caught three of his four looks for 36 yards and a grown-man touchdown.

He’ll have a good shot at finding the end zone again in a shootout with the 49ers next week.

Michael Mayer, Raiders

Brock Bowers suffered an ankle injury in Week 10 and did not return. Head coach Klint Kubiak could only tell reporters that he will be evaluated on Monday. Given his injury history, it would surprise me if he doesn't miss time. That puts Michael Mayer back into the starting mix, though he was already seeing plenty of run as the team’s inline tight end, with Bowers simply operating as a wide receiver. Mayer earned a healthy 19 percent target share when Bowers was out for two games to start the year. He will be in the TE2 mix in Week 11.

item.title: Grumpy Old Buckeye: Nitpicking Ohio State’s 28-19 win over Northwestern
item.description: Ohio State beat Northwestern, but the Buckeyes made their own job harder than it needed to be for much of the afternoon
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to the column that is always more comfortable being critical after wins than losses. It’s been a minute.

The Buckeyes returned to the win column in a game that was every bit as annoying and messy as expected when the Northwestern Wildcats came to town. I must admit, I spent more time this week yelling at the in-game broadcast team than the team on the field, but there were plenty of things to yell at the Buckeyes, too.

Let’s get into it.

Leveling up the embarrassing play

When things aren’t going well, there’s little reason to go find new ways to look bad, but the Buckeyes managed that at the start of Saturday’s game.

After a promising start — with a defensive stop and competent ball movement down the field — Ohio State entered the red zone, which is a figurative term, as there is no actual color red on the field anywhere that would indicate the team should stop.

Luke Fahey dropped back to pass and Northwestern brought pressure. As a result, the true freshman rushed his thr0w, firing downfield to Chris Henry Jr. about a split second too early. Henry came out of his break and turned to look for the ball, only to see (up close) that it had already arrived, and in fact, was in the process of hitting him in the face.

That would have been embarrassment enough, but the ball bounced high into the air and made for an easy interception. To add insult to injury, the Buckeyes didn’t even line up correctly on the play, getting flagged for illegal formation.

The Wildcats wisely turned down the penalty and kept the ball.

Finish the job

Ohio State’s defense was ferocious on first and second downs, especially early in the game, but there are few things as annoying in watching a football game as when players jump around and celebrate stops on those downs like they’d just stuffed a fourth-down to win the game.

Northwestern converted three consecutive third downs on its second drive, with the first two having to cover eight yards each. Third-and-long situations are supposed to be where good defenses thrive.

On the third set of downs, Ohio State missed a sack on first down that ended up in a completed pass that gained seven yards and set up a short third down.

Good defenses do not let the 46th-ranked team in third-down conversions connect on three in a row to put the game’s first points on the board. However, since that’s what Ohio State’s defense did, I can only conclude this defense has some work to do, even though third down defense got better (mostly) in the second half.

Cavalcade of dumb

The following is just a quick, bullet-form section of things that made me yell out loud at my television. To recap those:

  • On the second offensive drive, Ohio State center Carson Hinzmann was flagged for a false start. This was not his first of the season. You can understand why a tackle worried about a pass rusher or a guard concrned about having to pull on a play might move early. The guy with the football in his hand to start the play shouldn’t be doing that.
  • Ohio State trailed after the first quarter solely because Jeremiah Smith ran into Bo Jackson, his own teammate, who was failing to block downfield. Smith in the open field is a cheat code, and that play has to go for six points. It’s not a good look for your running back to not be executing a block or for your star wide receiver to simply run into said running back.
  • Zion Grady made another third-and-long Northwestern conversion even worse with an egregious facemask on the man blocking him, adding 15 more yards to the end of the play. Grady should buy Kenyatta Jackson dinner, because the latter then made three consecutive plays, including a sack, to force the field goal that Grady helped set up.

Grow up, already!

Ohio State fans are spoiled, and most of us know it.

The Buckeyes have had so much good quarterback play over recent years that we’ve forgotten what growing pains look like. Even when C.J. Stroud had a few vocal non-ball-knowers calling for his benching early in his career, you could see that things would come together sooner rather than later.

Fahey is showing us what real growing pains look like.

Too many passes are seemingly unnecessarily inaccurate, and he loses his footwork too often, meaning he can complete three straight passes and still look terrible on the fourth.

One of his worst throws of Saturday’s game came at the start of the second half. Arthur Smith and Ryan Day called for a shot down the field and Jeremiah Smith had beaten double coverage.

Any throw leading the Big Ten’s new all-time leading receiver in [insert ALL OF THE categories here] would result in a touchdown. Instead, it came much closer to being an interception than a completed pass.

Fahey’s throws all day were of inconsistent. In the second half, he threw a poor pass intended for Smith on second-and-10 that the receiver — who would normally catch it — couldn’t go down and get, but there was no reason to throw it so low.

Fahey then sent another poor pass on third down toward Smith that forced him to jump, and he somehow managed to get the call that he stayed in bounds, although it looked for all the world like a double clutch. Later, Fahey threw another pass that was too flat and Smith couldn’t get his foot down in the end zone near the sideline, when a throw to the back pylon would have been a sure six points.

After a penalty forced Ohio State into a first-and-19 situation later in the second half, Fahey threw a terrible pass behind Nate Roberts that should have picked up a good chunk of yardage. Fahey then threw maybe his worst pass of the day on the ensuing third-and-12 after breaking free of the pocket.

Hopefully, these are throws that go away with more experience and more work on mechanics. Fahey has a gun, but right now his bullets can (and do) go anywhere.

Cavalcade of dumb, part II

Before we move on, here’s another set of things that made me yell impolite things at my television. Ready!?

  • Just moments after Fahey badly missed Jeremiah Smith to start the second half, Henry dropped a sure touchdown pass on a deep ball down the left.
  • Henry’s drop was followed by a terrible punt and even worse punt coverage, meaning that scapegoating the special teams coach did not make things better. Northwestern then decided to throw to a tight end that was completely invisible to the secondary most of the afternoon to set up an eventual touchdown (following another third-down conversion by the Wildcats).
  • That Wildcats touchdown was followed by another bad special teams play, as three different Buckeyes struggled to pick up the knuckleball kickoff, forcing the offense to start in poor field position again.
  • An Austin Siereveld penalty for a block in the back that was nowhere near necessary erased a good pickup on an end around — one of the Buckeyes’ most inventive play calls of the day therefore did not end up working out (but it should have).

I must invent a new category for what Legend Bey did

I don’t think anything I’ve written in this column over the decade(-ish) I’ve been writing it for various outlets has enraged me more than Legend Bey making a nice play and then taunting the Northwestern sideline afterward, completely undoing all the good he previously did.

After a decent pickup of nine yards, Bey was pushed out in front of the Wildcats’ bench. He thought it would be a good idea to celebrate this monumental achievement in sports by getting in the face of the entire opposing team.

Instead of a second-and-1 play, the Buckeyes then faced a second-and-16 situation. Fahey got sacked on the next play and the Buckeyes eventually punted.

Wait, I take all of the above in this section back, because it led to the best special teams play of the season — a Northwestern muffed punt.

Cavalcade of dumb, part III

Sigh. Just… sigh.

  • Devin Sanchez somehow managed to get hit in the back with a punt late in the third quarter. Braydon Brus recovered for Northwestern to extend a drive that had just gone three-and-out and had gained only one yard. The defense did well to force another three-and-out after the muffed punt, but Brandon Inniss fair caught it at the OSU 10-yard line, which turned out to be minus-33 yards from where the Buckeyes should have started their next offensive possession.
  • Kenyatta Jackson roughed the quarterback by hitting him in the facemask with both hands after the ball had clearly been thrown. That turned what would have been a third-and-long situation into a Northwestern first down.
  • Isaiah West turned a conservative play call designed to put the game away into hope for the Wildcats with one of the worst fumbles you’ll ever see. Not only did the game situation require two hands on the football to protect it — at all costs, even at the cost of yardage — but the Wildcats weren’t even trying to strip it away on the play. He simply carried it too nonchalantly and it came out after routine contact. The Wildcats were almost out of time, but the turnover game them a chance.
  • Ohio State’s defense again determined that tight ends are not eligible recievers that require any attention whatsoever, allowing Luke Dehnicke to pick up 41 yards to set up the final Northwestern score. That touchdown came on fourth-and-10 and the last play of the game, but it was still annoying.

That’ll do it for another week.

The Buckeyes got a win, but it was far from pretty, and nowhere near as comfortable as it could have been if even half of the preventable things above hadn’t happened. No team is perfect, and this team is more not perfect than most Ohio State squads we’ve seen in recent years.

It’s not all on the quarterback injury, but there are times when one wonders how Tavien St. Clair must look in practice if this is what we’re seeing on the field — correctable mistakes or not.

Next up is a trip to Lincoln to play the Nebraska Cornhuskers in a game that could be every bit as annoying and messy as Saturday’s win over Northwestern was.

The game kicks off at noon because of course it kicks off at noon.

item.title: ESPN likes the Bears to repeat as division champs, but it won’t be easy
item.description: There’s a 3-way tie atop the NFC North, but ESPN’s beat writer poll suggests the Bears will eventually pull away and repeat as champs.
item.content:encoded:
Well, that division lead was fun while it lasted.

The Chicago Bears (7-2), after entering their Week 10 bye at the top of the NFC North, are now suddenly third in the division following Sunday’s games. Minnesota (7-2), who’s beaten Chicago already this year and just dispatched Green Bay (6-4), and Detroit (7-2) now share the same record as the Bears but own tiebreakers (for now). 

Still, a number of experts think the Bears remain the best team in the North—or at least they did before the Vikings and their newly re-acquired quarterback Kirk Cousins put the beats on the Packers 30-10 yesterday. 

In a pre-Week 10 pundit poll of the NFC North’s ESPN beat writers, three of four put the Bears atop their ultimate NFC North rankings.

“The Bears’ runway coming out of the bye is favorable with the Saints in Week 11 and the lowly Dolphins in Week 14, but Chicago has four division opponents (after an 0-2 start in NFC North play) and two potential Super Bowl previews with the Jaguars and Bills. Still, the Bears have proved they can win ugly and coach Ben Johnson is 7-0 in November since arriving in Chicago. With the most complete team in the division and an offense scoring 30.7 points per game when Williams has been under center, the Bears are in position to capture the division crown again,” said Courtney Cronin.

“The Bears have the most well-rounded team in the division, and maybe the conference, following the trade for Simmons. But the one thing to watch is that both of their losses this season were in the division. That could be detrimental in a division tiebreaker if that is how the season ends,” Kevin Seifert, a Vikings insider, added.

Rob Demovsky, notably of the Packers beat, even gave the Bears their props.

“The Bears are the best team in the division despite being 0-2. They ran into Minnesota’s red-hot early-season defense in Week 2 and played without their quarterback in Week 5 at Green Bay. They haven’t even played the Lions yet, and Green Bay still has to go to Soldier Field as part of the three-game finishing stretch for the Bears that goes Packers at home, Lions at home and Vikings on the road,” he said.

Only Lions writer Eric Woodyard shot down the Bears hype, saying—you guessed it—the Lions were the better squad.

“The Bears might be the most well-rounded team in the division, but the Lions beat them twice last season, as Campbell could be one of the few coaches who knows how to counter the attack of Johnson—his former offensive coordinator. The division is certainly up for grabs, but Detroit’s explosive offense could be the game-changer in the division title race,” he wrote. 

Though this year is not last year, of course, it’s not hard to see how much trouble Detroit has given these Ben Johnson-led Bears. Even with Chicago adding Jeffery Simmons and the Lions now likely to lose Aidan Hutchinson for an extended period of time—maybe even the season—Detroit has been too good to dismiss.

And while none of the writers envisioned Cousins putting Minnesota over the top, watching his performance in his first game back with Kevin O’Connell and the Vikings makes one curious.

As for the Packers? See you at Soldier Field on Christmas. Payback time.

The Bears will have every opportunity to prove those writers right with four division games in the back stretch of their season. If they can so much as break even against their North opponents for the season, it would get them to 10 wins. But who knows? 10 wins might not be enough to keep their crown.

Time to see what Johnson, Caleb Williams, and this squad are made of.

item.title: Cowboys vs. 49ers Stock Report: Caleb Downs has rough day
item.description: Here is our stock report following Sunday’s loss to San Francisco
item.content:encoded:
The scoreboard can often lie. On Sunday, the final between the Dallas Cowboys and San Francisco 49ers read 46-40 in favor of the visiting Niners, but anyone who watched the game knows that it was in no way that close.

It is a stretch to call Dallas’ flurry late in the game “garbage time,” but it all came when San Francisco was clearly ready to get on a plane and head home. The point is that nothing felt seriously in doubt.

You only lose games so soundly, regardless of what the scoreboard said as noted, because of a collective failure from people involved. It should come as no surprise that our stock report is filled with more downs than ups as a result of it all.

Let’s begin.

Stock Down: Brian Schottenheimer

We say it every week. What more is there to say?

The scoreboard is a liar as noted, so it is in no way like Brian Schottenheimer had his team ready to play. What’s more is that he saw them take another third quarter off so that the game got out of hand, and then everybody started caring as time was running out in the fourth quarter.

Maybe if the Cowboys were better we’d give Schotty a pass for this being the big, bad San Francisco 49ers. But you know what? They are the big, bad 49ers. Someone has to stand up and make Dallas respectable to a team they were once proper and legitimate rivals with. Someone has to be the head coach that has a second winning streak before Thanksgiving of his second season.

Those people were not Brian Schottenheimer this week.

Stock Down: Christian Parker

It is Kyle Shanahan. We know that. But goodness.

The Dallas Cowboys defense appeared to be taking a few steps these last few weeks, but we were cautious because of the quality of opposing quarterbacks they played. It turns out that context mattered.

I’ve long been against moving on from Parker because the defense needs consistency at some point. But what is there to hang your hat on? How can you justify what is happening? In what world?

Stock Down: Caleb Downs

This was far and away Caleb Downs’ worst game as a professional. It unfortunately came a week after his best.

I guess that’s what happens when you are tasked with hanging on for dear life against George Kittle. Downs fell short of that challenge, but at least unlike the rest of his defensive teammates, he can still say he is learning all of this on the fly.

Still though, we really hyped Downs up over the offseason. We believed he was ready for this. On Sunday he wasn’t.

Stock Down: Cobie Durant

Caleb was one of two Cowboys defenders to get completely run over by San Francisco’s Kaelon Black as Cobie Durant was the other.

The Cowboys are never ready for the physical fight that is the 49ers. Never. It is a shame.

Stock Down: All linebackers

It was impossible to boil this down to just one.

San Francisco is very talented, but notably they are exceptionally well-coached. Kyle Shanahan had every Cowboys linebacker criss-crossing themselves all day with all of his uses of motion and play action.

On the second Deebo Samuel touchdown, literally 10 Cowboys players bought the fake and left Joey Porter Jr. on one side to take on what Tom Brady called a red wave.

You can’t get got every time.

Stock Down: KaVontae Turpin

He had a drop of a pass that landed squarely in his hands. How does that even happen?

Remember when Turpin was regarded to be a special teams ace, though? Remember when he was providing the team with an elite advantage?

Where is that? What is he offering that anyone else can’t from a return game standpoint? I will take any answer.

Stock Down: Brandon Aubrey

His only miss in this game was an extra point, but the point (no pun intended) is that he missed yet another kick.

We are sort of running out of excuses for Aubrey at this point. It can’t always be this, that, or whatever is convenient. He is the top-paid kicker in the NFL and he is in no way among the most reliable kickers in the league right now. His miss was an extra point as noted in this game. An extra point! At home! Indoors!

The Cowboys hardly lost because of that missed point, but these keep piling up.

Stock Up: Quinnen Williams

The Cowboys absolutely have a war daddy.

Quinnen Williams might be the best player on the Cowboys period right now. He did his best to singlehandedly save the team at the end as he forced a fumble that almost made the attempted rally actually possible.

It is legitimately impressive how Quinnen is not allowing the state of things to impact his effort. I suppose spending a ton of time with the New York Jets will harden you in that way.

Stock Up: George Pickens

Let’s state that the taunting penalty was silly. We all agree.

But wow what a game from George Pickens. He essentially was the entire offense for much of the game, at least before it got away from Dallas and they were playing catch up.

It is hard to wonder what could or would have happened if this performance came right before the trade deadline. It didn’t, though. And now he and Dallas are stuck with each other until contract negotiations that will surely be calm and easy.

Stock Up: LT Overton

In addition to Quinnen Williams the Cowboys also saw some force up front from one of their rookies in LT Overton, including an impressive batted pass.

If the Cowboys are ever going to find true and proper form in the future it is going to be because they develop a bevy of options along the defensive line. Hopefully Overton is a part of that future alongside Quinnen Williams and whoever else the Cowboys fan find between now and that hypothetical day.

item.title: Rams’ Sean McVay is re-inventing offense again due to injuries
item.description: McVay continues to reinvent the Rams offense when it needs new life
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams have never been afraid to get creative with their offensive personnel groupings, and injuries are once again forcing Sean McVay to think outside the box. What started with 11 personnel has evolved into 13 personnel and, most recently, 20 personnel as the Rams continue searching for ways to keep their offense productive despite losing key playmakers.

McVay’s ability to adapt when his back is against the wall is one of his greatest strengths as a head coach. Rather than stubbornly sticking to an offensive identity that no longer fits the available personnel, McVay has consistently found ways to maximize the players at his disposal. The Rams’ latest adjustment is simply another example of that creativity.

11 personnel

In 2017, McVay began building an offense around 11 personnel, featuring one running back, one tight end, and three wide receivers. Cooper Kupp was an important piece of that identity. During training camp, McVay recognized Kupp’s ability to operate in tight spaces and perform some of the responsibilities traditionally associated with a tight end while maintaining the route-running finesse of a wide receiver.

Kupp’s versatility helped make the formation so difficult to defend. The Rams could spread defenses out while still having receivers capable of winning underneath and creating opportunities after the catch.

The Rams dominated the NFL in 11 personnel usage from 2017-2024. Since the data was tracked from 2021-2024 by Sharp Football Analysis, LA led the NFL with 89% of their play calls.

13 personnel

Fast forward to 2025, and McVay found another way to reinvent his offense. After losing Puka Nacua to injury, including his absence against the Jacksonville Jaguars in London, the Rams leaned into 13 personnel, featuring one running back and three tight ends. The Rams used Camden Yards in Baltimore to test their new personnel change and since then, the Rams have been at the forefront of leading the NFL in 13 usage.

Rather than trying to replace Nacua’s production with another traditional receiver, McVay used his tight ends to create mismatches, establish the running game, and give Matthew Stafford different throwing windows. What initially looked like an injury-driven adjustment became a legitimate offensive identity.

20 personnel

Now, in Week 10 against the Arizona Cardinals, McVay introduced another wrinkle. With Terrance Ferguson, Nacua, and Davante Adams unavailable, the Rams turned to 20 personnel, featuring two running backs and three wide receivers.

The grouping gave the Rams another way to create offensive opportunities without relying on their depleted tight end and receiver rooms. Los Angeles used the grouping for 17 plays, generating 197 yards and a touchdown.

Three different personnel identities, all built around the same philosophy. McVay doesn’t need a perfect roster to manufacture an effective offense. He just needs to find another way to attack.
